title: Labels on a graph
objectives: Train a graph network to label nodes from a few known labels, and see deep layers over-smooth.

screens.title: Guess the rest
screens.prose: 40 firms in two seeded communities: a pair in the same community is linked with chance 0.3, a pair across with chance 0.03. Only firms 0 and 1 (blue) and 20 and 21 (orange) have known labels. Firm 3 has no label, and its first number, 1.88, is typical of the orange community.
screens.question: Which label would you give firm 3?

options.text: Blue, because all 5 of its links go to the left-hand cluster
Orange, because its first number is typical of orange firms
options.why: One noisy number is weak evidence. Firm 3's links point to the blue side, and links within a community are 10 times as likely.

options.text: Neither: with no label it cannot be guessed
options.why: The links carry information: they are far more common inside a community.

options.text: Orange, because it sits nearest to firm 20
options.why: Position on the drawing is only a layout. Count its links instead.

hints.text: Look at where firm 3's links go.
All 5 of its links go to blue-side firms.

feedback.correct: Blue: all 5 of firm 3's links go to its own side, and it is indeed blue.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count firm 3's links on each side.

explain.text: Links inside a community are ten times as likely as across, so a firm whose 5 links all go to the blue side is very likely blue. A graph network will use exactly this.

screens.title: Averaging over the graph
screens.prose: Each firm has two noisy numbers. Slide to replace them by $\hat{\mathbf A}\mathbf X$, then $\hat{\mathbf A}^2\mathbf X$ and $\hat{\mathbf A}^4\mathbf X$: each firm averaged with its neighbours.

state.caption: Raw numbers, coloured by the true community.

frames.caption: Raw numbers, coloured by the true community.

screens.question: After two averaging steps, how do the two clouds compare with the raw numbers?

options.text: They overlap far less: a firm's neighbours are mostly its own kind, so their noise cancels
They overlap just as much, since averaging only shrinks the numbers
options.why: Averaging shrinks the noise more than the gap, because the neighbours share the community's mean.

options.text: They overlap more, because the links mix the communities
options.why: Only a few links cross; most average a firm with its own community.

options.text: The two clouds swap sides
options.why: Averaging keeps each community's mean where it was; it does not flip signs.

hints.text: Compare the frames for 0 and 2 steps.
Watch the gap between the colours along number 1.

feedback.correct: They pull apart: the noise averages out, the community's mean does not.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Slide between 0 and 2 steps and compare the overlap.

explain.text: A firm's neighbours are mostly in its own community, so averaging keeps the community mean and cancels much of the noise. The clouds separate along number 1, where the communities differ.

screens.title: Train on four, label forty
screens.prose: Name it: **semi-supervised node classification**. The two-layer network of l19, with 16 hidden numbers, is trained on the cross-entropy of firms 0, 1, 20 and 21 only, for 200 Adam steps. Through $\hat{\mathbf A}$ the other firms still shape every prediction. The colours show its labels; the highlighted firm is wrong.
screens.question: What is its accuracy on the 36 firms without a label? Give 3 decimal places.

hints.text: Count the unlabelled firms it gets right.
35 of the 36.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count only the 36 firms that had no label.

byKey.all: You counted the four training firms as well, out of 40. Their labels were given, so they say nothing.
byKey.wrong-share: That is the share it gets wrong.

explain.text: Only 4 labels entered the loss, yet the network labels 35 of the other 36 firms correctly, 0.972. The links carried the labels' information to the rest. The unlabelled firms' numbers and links were used in training, but not their labels, so the score is for this graph: a new graph needs its own check.

screens.title: Without the graph
screens.prose: Replace $\hat{\mathbf A}$ by $\mathbf I$ and the same network becomes a per-node network: each firm is judged on its own two numbers, as at the isolated firm of l19. Trained the same way on the same four firms, it labels 21 of the 36 correctly.
screens.question: How many more of the 36 firms does the graph network label correctly?

hints.text: The graph network gets 35 right.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Subtract the per-node network's count from the graph network's.

byKey.mlp-wrong: That is how many the per-node network gets wrong. Compare the two counts right.
byKey.gcn: That is the graph network's own count.

explain.text: With four labels and noisy numbers, the per-node network is close to a coin toss (0.58). The graph network borrows strength from neighbours and gets 14 more right; over 20 graphs the means are 0.95 and 0.60.

screens.title: A perfect score
screens.prose: A colleague trains both networks and reports accuracy 1.0 for each, measured on firms 0, 1, 20 and 21.
screens.question: What does the 1.0 tell you?

options.text: Nothing about the other 36: the loss was fitted on those four
That the two networks are equally good at the task
options.why: On the 36 unlabelled firms they score 0.97 and 0.58. The training firms cannot tell them apart.

options.text: That the graph carries no extra information at all
options.why: Both fit four points easily. The graph's value shows only on firms the loss never saw.

options.text: That both networks have failed and need more data
options.why: Fitting the training firms is expected. The question is how they do on the rest.

hints.text: Which firms' labels did the loss use?
Measure on the firms the network never saw a label for.

feedback.correct: Nothing: those four labels were the training data.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask which firms the loss was fitted on.

byKey.equal: You read equal training scores as equal networks. On the 36 unlabelled firms they score 0.97 and 0.58.

explain.text: A network fits its four training labels almost always, so their accuracy measures nothing. Report accuracy on the firms whose labels the loss never used.

screens.title: Too many steps
screens.prose: Stack more averaging and the firms blur together. The cleanest test is linear: average $k$ times, then one weight matrix, $\hat{\mathbf A}^k\mathbf X\mathbf W$, trained on the same four firms. The bars give the mean accuracy over 20 seeded graphs.
screens.question: At how many averaging steps is the mean accuracy highest?

hints.text: Read the tallest bar.
It is 0.97.

feedback.correct: 8 steps, at 0.97; by 128 steps it is 0.50, a coin toss.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the tallest bar.

byKey.two: Two steps is what our two-layer network uses, at 0.91. The tallest bar is further right.
byKey.most: 128 steps gives 0.50, a coin toss. More averaging past the peak hurts.

explain.text: Accuracy rises to 0.97 at 8 steps, then falls to 0.50: **over-smoothing**, with no ReLU involved. A 16-layer ReLU network scores a mean of 0.55: 17 of its 20 runs predict one class, and in 11 every last-layer unit is dead, so the output is 0. Dead units and over-smoothing both collapse a deep stack, and the training loss stays above 0.6 in 14 runs.

screens.title: Links that ignore the labels
screens.prose: Now link every pair with the same chance, 0.165, whatever the community. The firms and numbers are unchanged; only the links stop following the labels.
screens.question: What does the second pair of bars show?

options.text: The gain needs links that follow the labels: test that first
A graph network always beats a per-node network on a graph
options.why: On the graph with no signal it scores 0.57 against 0.60: no gain.

options.text: The training failed on the second graph, so it should be rerun
options.why: Training ran the same way. The links simply carry no label information.

options.text: More links of the same kind would fix the problem
options.why: Adding links that ignore the labels mixes the communities further.

hints.text: Compare the graph network's two bars.
When links ignore labels, averaging mixes firms from both sides.

feedback.correct: The gain needs links that follow the labels. Here it vanishes.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the graph network with and without signal in the links.

explain.text: With links that ignore the labels, the graph network scores 0.57, no better than the per-node network's 0.60. Comparing against a per-node network is the honest check that the graph carries signal.

screens.title: What we trained, and where it ends
screens.prose:
We minimised the cross-entropy over the labelled set $T$ only:

$$L = -\frac{1}{|T|}\sum_{i \in T} \log \operatorname{softmax}\big(\hat{\mathbf A}\operatorname{ReLU}(\hat{\mathbf A}\mathbf X\mathbf W_1)\mathbf W_2\big)_{i, y_i}.$$

Many steps of $\hat{\mathbf A}$ keep only its top eigenvector, with entries $\propto \sqrt{\tilde d_i}$ (`eigen` l4). Firm 2 has 1 link and firm 17 has 10.
screens.question: After many steps, firm 2's row is what multiple of firm 17's? Give 3 decimal places.

hints.text: With self-loops the degrees are 2 and 11.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Take the square root of the ratio of the degrees with self-loops.

byKey.no-root: You took the ratio of the degrees. The eigenvector holds their square roots.
byKey.no-loop: You used the degrees without self-loops.
byKey.equal: You expected every row to become equal. With $\hat{\mathbf A}$ the rows line up but scale with $\sqrt{\tilde d_i}$.

explain.text: In the limit every row points the same way, scaled by $\sqrt{\tilde d_i}$, so the rows differ only by degree, here 0.426. The communities are gone, which is why deep averaging labels no better than a coin.

screens.prose: Write `planted_partition(n, p_in, p_out, seed)`, the generator behind this lesson's graphs. Nodes 0 to $n/2 - 1$ (rounded down) form community 0. widget.solution:
import numpy as np


def planted_partition(n, p_in, p_out, seed):
    U = np.random.default_rng(seed).random((n, n))
    y = (np.arange(n) >= n // 2).astype(int)
    P = np.where(y[:, None] == y[None, :], p_in, p_out)
    A = np.triu((U < P).astype(float), 1)
    return A + A.T, y

import numpy as np
from autograd import Tensor, cross_entropy
from nt_ops_l1 import adam_step


def train_gcn(A_hat, X, y, train_idx, steps, lr, seed):
    A_hat = np.asarray(A_hat, dtype=float)
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    y = np.asarray(y)
    tr = np.asarray(train_idx)
    K = int(y.max()) + 1
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    W = [rng.standard_normal((X.shape[1], 16)) / np.sqrt(X.shape[1]),
         rng.standard_normal((16, K)) / np.sqrt(16)]
    m = [np.zeros_like(w) for w in W]
    v = [np.zeros_like(w) for w in W]
    losses = []
    for t in range(1, steps + 1):
        W1, W2 = Tensor(W[0]), Tensor(W[1])
        logits = A_hat @ (A_hat @ X @ W1).relu() @ W2
        loss = cross_entropy(logits[tr], y[tr])
        loss.backward()
        losses.append(loss.item())
        W, m, v = adam_step(W, [W1.grad, W2.grad], m, v, t, lr)
    pred = (A_hat @ np.maximum(A_hat @ X @ W[0], 0) @ W[1]).argmax(axis=1)
    other = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(len(y)), tr)
    return float(np.mean(pred[other] == y[other])), losses

        W1, W2 = Tensor(W[0]), Tensor(W[1])
        logits = A_hat @ (A_hat @ X @ W1).relu() @ W2
        loss = cross_entropy(logits[tr], y[tr])
        loss.backward()
        losses.append(loss.item())
        acc = float(np.mean(logits.data.argmax(axis=1)[other] == y[other]))
        if acc > best:
            best, bestW = acc, W
        W, m, v = adam_step(W, [W1.grad, W2.grad], m, v, t, lr)
    W = bestW
    pred = (A_hat @ np.maximum(A_hat @ X @ W[0], 0) @ W[1]).argmax(axis=1)
    other = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(len(y)), tr)
    return float(np.mean(pred[other] == y[other])), losses
mutants.symptom: Keeps the weights of the step with the best accuracy on the unlabelled nodes, which uses labels the task does not have.

import numpy as np
from autograd import Tensor, cross_entropy
from nt_ops_l1 import adam_step


def train_gcn(A_hat, X, y, train_idx, steps, lr, seed):
    A_hat = np.asarray(A_hat, dtype=float)
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    y = np.asarray(y)
    tr = np.asarray([0, 1, 20, 21])
    K = int(y.max()) + 1
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    W = [rng.standard_normal((X.shape[1], 16)) / np.sqrt(X.shape[1]),
         rng.standard_normal((16, K)) / np.sqrt(16)]
    m = [np.zeros_like(w) for w in W]
    v = [np.zeros_like(w) for w in W]
    losses = []
    for t in range(1, steps + 1):
        W1, W2 = Tensor(W[0]), Tensor(W[1])
        logits = A_hat @ (A_hat @ X @ W1).relu() @ W2
        loss = cross_entropy(logits[tr], y[tr])
        loss.backward()
        losses.append(loss.item())
        W, m, v = adam_step(W, [W1.grad, W2.grad], m, v, t, lr)
    pred = (A_hat @ np.maximum(A_hat @ X @ W[0], 0) @ W[1]).argmax(axis=1)
    other = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(len(y)), tr)
    return float(np.mean(pred[other] == y[other])), losses

screens.title: Measure the blur
screens.prose: Write `feature_spread(A_hat, X, depth)`. For $k = 0, \ldots, \text{depth}$ take $\mathbf Z = \hat{\mathbf A}^k\mathbf X$ and report the share of $\mathbf Z$ outside the top eigenvector $\mathbf v$ of $\hat{\mathbf A}$: $\lVert\mathbf Z - \mathbf v\mathbf v^\top\mathbf Z\rVert / \lVert\mathbf Z\rVert$. The bars show it for the lesson's graph.
screens.question: Write `feature_spread`.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np


def feature_spread(A_hat, X, depth):
    A_hat = np.asarray(A_hat, dtype=float)
    Z = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    lam, V = np.linalg.eigh(A_hat)
    v = V[:, -1]
    out = []
    for k in range(depth + 1):
        out.append(float(np.linalg.norm(Z - np.outer(v, v @ Z)) / np.linalg.norm(Z)))
        Z = A_hat @ Z
    return out

hints.text: `np.linalg.eigh` returns eigenvalues in rising order, so the top eigenvector is the last column.
Multiply by $\hat{\mathbf A}$ once per step: `Z = A_hat @ Z`.

feedback.correct: Your spreads match: near 1 at first, about 0.69 at 8 steps, and 0 by 128.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Use the eigenvector of the largest eigenvalue (the last column from `eigh`), multiply by $\hat{\mathbf A}$ once a step rather than raising its entries to a power, measure the part outside $\mathbf v$, and divide by $\lVert\mathbf Z\rVert$, and not the spread around the mean row: rows that line up along $\mathbf v$ still differ by $\sqrt{\tilde d_i}$.

explain.text: The share outside $\mathbf v$ shrinks like the second eigenvalue to the power $k$. When it reaches 0 the rows differ only by $\sqrt{\tilde d_i}$, and the communities are gone.

screens.title: Sectors of unlisted firms
screens.prose: A desk wants the sector of 2,000 unlisted firms from 150 known ones, using a supply-chain network. On held-out known firms a graph network scores 0.71, a per-node network 0.70, and the graph network on links shuffled at random 0.70.
screens.question: What should the desk conclude?

options.text: The links add almost nothing, so the graph is not yet to be trusted
Use the graph network, since it has the best of the three scores
options.why: 0.71 against 0.70 is within noise, and shuffled links do as well. The graph shows no signal.

options.text: Add layers so the graph network sees further
options.why: More layers average more and blur further. Depth cannot add signal the links lack.

options.text: Report the training accuracy instead, which is higher
options.why: Training accuracy says nothing about firms whose labels the loss never saw.

hints.text: Compare the graph network with both baselines.
Shuffled links keep every firm's degree but link firms at random, whatever their sector.

feedback.correct: The links carry little sector information here; check other link types first.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what the graph adds over the two baselines.

explain.text: A graph network earns its place only when it beats the per-node network and the shuffled-links network on held-out firms. Here the 0.01 gap is noise, so the links do not yet carry the sector.

ideas: Semi-supervised node classification fits the cross-entropy of a few labelled nodes; through $\hat{\mathbf A}$ the links carry their information to the rest, and accuracy is measured only on the unlabelled nodes.
A graph network beats a per-node network only when links follow the labels, so compare the two (and shuffled links) before trusting the graph.
Many averaging steps keep only the top eigenvector of $\hat{\mathbf A}$, with entries $\propto\sqrt{\tilde d_i}$ on a connected graph, so deep stacks over-smooth and the communities blur.

formula.name: Over-smoothing
formula.tex: \hat{\mathbf A}^k\mathbf X \to \mathbf v\mathbf v^\top\mathbf X, \qquad v_i \propto \sqrt{\tilde d_i}
formula.note: On a connected graph, as $k$ grows.

quiz.question: What accuracy should be reported? Give a decimal.

quiz.prose: A team applies $\hat{\mathbf A}$ 40 times to a connected graph's features, then fits one weight matrix, and finds every node predicted in the same class.
quiz.question: What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Repeated averaging left only the top eigenvector: nodes differ by degree
The learning rate was too small to separate the two classes in time
options.why: A larger rate cannot restore differences the averaging has removed.

options.text: The graph has too few nodes for so deep a network to learn from
options.why: Size is not the cause: 40 multiplications by $\hat{\mathbf A}$ blur any connected graph.

options.text: ReLU removes every negative feature, so the classes look alike
options.why: This stack has no ReLU, and 40 multiplications by $\hat{\mathbf A}$ still leave only the top eigenvector.

feedback.correct: Over-smoothing: $\hat{\mathbf A}^{40}$ keeps little more than the top eigenvector.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about what 40 multiplications by $\hat{\mathbf A}$ do, with no ReLU in sight.

explain.text: Each multiplication by $\hat{\mathbf A}$ blurs the features; after many, they lie along the top eigenvector, which carries only $\sqrt{\tilde d_i}$. A deep ReLU stack can also collapse by dead units: in this level's 16-layer runs, 11 of 20 ended with every last-layer unit dead.

quiz.prose: On a connected graph, node $a$ has 3 links and node $b$ has 15. Repeated multiplication by $\hat{\mathbf A}$ runs for many steps.
quiz.question: What multiple of $b$'s row does $a$'s row become? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Use $\sqrt{\tilde d_a / \tilde d_b}$ with the self-loops counted.

byKey.no-root: You took the ratio of degrees, $4/16$. The eigenvector holds their square roots.
byKey.no-loop: You left out the self-loops: the degrees are 4 and 16.

explain.text: With self-loops the degrees are 4 and 16, and the top eigenvector's entries are $\propto\sqrt{\tilde d_i}$, so the ratio is 0.5.
